title: Northgate Logistics Redesigns Its Weekly Report
description: An operations team uses Claude to halve the time its weekly depot report takes without losing leadership's trust in the numbers. They choose an output format and a model for each task, decide whether to augment or redesign the workflow, trace a wrong figure, judge whether the faster process is really an optimisation, and report the results to leadership.

scenario.background: Northgate Logistics' operations team has a mandate to halve the time its weekly performance report takes, as long as leadership trusts the numbers as much as before. The company runs four regional depots, and every Monday the team spends most of a day copying figures from three spreadsheets, writing a commentary for each depot and pasting it all into a slide deck for the leadership meeting. Each depot manager then receives an emailed summary. The team has Claude on an Enterprise plan. After six weeks, Priya must report the results to the leadership team.

characters.name: Priya Nair
characters.concern: She owns the report and needs leadership to trust the figures as much as they do today.

characters.name: Jonas Weber
characters.concern: He spends most Mondays building the report and wants to spend that time on analysis instead.

characters.name: Amara Osei
characters.concern: She wants a short summary of her depot's numbers and actions, not the whole leadership deck.

characters.name: Daniel Price
characters.concern: He reconciles the cost figures and has caught copying errors in past reports.

questions.stem: Jonas wants Claude to pull each depot's on-time rate, cost per parcel and incident count from the three spreadsheets into one place that he'll paste into the leadership deck's data table. Which output format should he ask for?
options: A short narrative paragraph for each depot, covering its three measures in a fixed order
An interactive dashboard artifact with a chart for each of the three measures
A table with one row per depot and one column per measure
A bullet list giving each depot's figures on a single line, separated by commas
questions.explanation: Format follows the next step. C is correct: the figures are going straight into the deck's data table, so one row per depot and one column per measure pastes in without retyping. A is wrong because figures in prose have to be re-keyed into the table by hand. B is wrong because a dashboard is more than this step needs and doesn't paste into the deck's table. D is wrong because one line per depot loses the column structure the table needs.

questions.stem: The report needs two kinds of Claude work: routine extraction and formatting of the same figures each week, and a short commentary on why one depot's costs rose, drawing on conflicting signals in the data. How should Jonas choose models?
options: A lighter model for the extraction, and a more capable model or higher effort for the commentary, tested on a few weeks' data
The most capable model at maximum effort for both tasks, so the figures leadership sees get the most careful treatment
The fastest model for both tasks, since halving the report's time is the mandate leadership has set for the team
One mid-range model at its default effort for both tasks, so the outputs stay consistent from one week to the next
questions.explanation: Pick the model per task and test it. A is correct: routine extraction is simple and repeats each week, so a lighter model suits it, while the cost commentary needs reasoning over conflicting signals, so it gets higher effort or a more capable model; a few weeks' sample confirms both. B is wrong because it spends time and usage on routine work. C is wrong because the mandate also requires trusted analysis. D is wrong because consistency doesn't make one setting right for two different tasks.

questions.stem: Priya considers two options: add Claude to the current process to draft the commentary, or redesign it so one validated data extract feeds the table, the commentary and each depot manager's summary. When is the redesign the better choice?
options: When the team has grown comfortable using Claude after drafting the weekly commentary for a few weeks running
When the repeated copying is there just because of manual limits, and Daniel's reconciliation check stays
When the redesign removes the largest number of steps from the Monday process, Daniel's check included
When Claude can also sign off the finished report, so leadership receives it earlier on a Monday
questions.explanation: Redesign when steps exist because of manual limits, and keep the checks. B is correct: copying the same figures into a table, a deck and emails exists because people did it by hand, so one validated extract can feed all three outputs, while Daniel's check keeps leadership's trust. A is wrong because comfort isn't evidence that a step should change. C is wrong because removing the check trades trust for time. D is wrong because sign-off stays with accountable people.

questions.stem: Four weeks into the redesign, Daniel finds a wrong cost-per-parcel figure in 2 of the last 4 depot summaries; the leadership table is right. The summaries run on the lighter model chosen for routine work. What should Priya do first?
options: Move each step of the report to the most capable model, since the errors started after the redesign went live
Drop the depot summaries from the redesign, since the leadership table is the part that matters most
Add "check your maths carefully" to the summary prompt, then rerun the two summaries that were wrong
Trace the two figures back through the extract and the source spreadsheet, then change one thing and retest
questions.explanation: Trace a wrong figure before changing anything. D is correct: comparing the figures with the validated extract and the source spreadsheet shows where they went wrong. Here the extract is right and the lighter model mis-summed two cost lines in the summary step, so that one step is what to change before retesting the same summaries. A is wrong because it changes everything without knowing the cause. B is wrong because it drops output depot managers use. C is wrong because Claude checking itself isn't verification.

questions.stem: The trace confirms that the lighter model mis-summed cost lines in the summary step. The report now takes two hours instead of a day. How should Priya treat the redesign?
options: Count it as a success and keep it unchanged, since the time target was met and the leadership table was right
Keep the time saving, move the summary step back to the more capable setting or add a figure check, and sample weekly
Return to the old Monday process, since cost errors in the summaries have shaken confidence in the whole of the redesign
Keep the redesign and drop Daniel's reconciliation check, which now takes more time than any other step
questions.explanation: A faster process isn't finished until quality matches. B is correct: the time saving is real, but summaries with wrong costs aren't an optimisation, so Priya fixes the one step the trace pointed to, keeps the rest, and samples quality weekly to confirm it holds. A is wrong because errors would keep reaching depot managers. C is wrong because it throws away the parts that work. D is wrong because Daniel's check is what caught the errors.

questions.stem: After six weeks, Priya presents the results to the leadership team, who will decide whether to extend the approach to the monthly report. What should her update contain?
options: Before-and-after time on the same report, the two errors and how the check caught them, what Claude can't see, and a next step
The time saved each Monday, followed by a live demo of Claude writing commentary for a made-up depot to show how it works
The time saved, plus a commitment that the summary errors are fixed for good, so leadership can extend the approach with confidence
The time saved and the analysis hours Jonas has gained, leaving out the two errors because they have already been fixed
questions.explanation: Show measured results and plain limits. A is correct: leadership needs before-and-after time on the same report, the errors and how review caught them, what Claude can't do (it sees only the extract it's given), the checks that stay, and a recommendation to extend to the monthly report. B is wrong because a made-up depot isn't evidence. C is wrong because promising no further errors breaks trust at the first one. D is wrong because hiding the errors leaves leadership unable to judge the risk.

keyLearnings: Format follows the next step: data headed for a table should come out as rows and columns.
Pick the model per task, and test the choice on a sample before relying on it.
Redesign when steps exist because of manual limits, and keep the checks that maintain trust.
Trace a wrong figure before changing anything, because a faster process isn't finished until quality matches.
